result: Myomatrix arrays are a novel class of high-density, flexible electrode devices that enable stable recordings from individual motor units during natural behaviors across multiple species including mice, rats, primates, songbirds, frogs, and insects.
evaluation: All three reviewers explicitly affirm this core finding. The editor states this is an 'important paper' reporting 'major technical advances for in vivo intramuscular electrical recording from multiple motor units in behaving animals' with 'compelling demonstrations of the efficacy of this new technique in multiple animal species.' Reviewers note 'the main significance of this manuscript is the application of this new technology to different muscles and animal species during naturalistic behaviors' and praise 'convincing examples of EMG recordings with high signal quality using this new technology from a wide array of animal species, muscles, and behavior.'

result: Traditional EMG methods have significant limitations: they require restricted movements (typically isometric tasks), fine-wire electrodes cannot detect single motor units in small muscles like those of mice or songbirds, and current methods for observing motor output lag behind neural recording technologies.
evaluation: Reviewers accept these motivating claims about the limitations of existing methods without challenge. One reviewer explicitly states that 'neurophysiology faces an urgent need for methods to record their activity at high resolution and scale in intact animals during natural movement' and that 'current methods of recording EMG using intramuscular fine-wire electrodes do not allow for isolation of motor units and are limited by the muscle size and the type of behavior.' These claims provide accepted context for the significance of the new technology.

result: Myomatrix arrays routinely isolated individual motor units during mouse locomotion, whereas fine-wire EMG from reanalyzed datasets (Miri et al., 2017) never isolated individual motor units. Myomatrix arrays also showed significantly higher signal-to-noise ratios than fine-wire EMG (p=0.002 when all data pooled).
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm the superior performance of Myomatrix over traditional methods. One reviewer states 'the claims are justified by the data' and another notes 'convincing examples of EMG recordings with high signal quality.' The direct comparison with fine-wire EMG and statistical evidence of superior SNR is accepted without critique, supporting the claim that Myomatrix represents a substantial technical advance over existing methods.

result: At least four Myomatrix threads bearing 32 electrodes total can be inserted into one mouse muscle, greatly expanding recording channels compared to traditional fine-wire EMG which typically provides only a single bipolar channel per mouse muscle.
evaluation: Reviewers accept this claim as part of the demonstrated technical advantages. One reviewer specifically highlights 'the design included suture holes and pull-on tabs that facilitate implantation and ensure stable recordings over months' as a strength. The multi-channel capability is implicitly endorsed through reviewers' acceptance of the multi-unit recordings shown throughout the manuscript.

result: Myomatrix arrays maintained stable single-unit recordings over extended periods: up to 4791 stride cycles in mice (10-60 min sessions), 1292 reaching trials in primates (97 min), and individual motor units were recorded up to 65 days post-implantation, with recording duration limited by animal behavior rather than signal loss.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm recording stability as a key strength. One reviewer notes 'the design included suture holes and pull-on tabs that facilitate implantation and ensure stable recordings over months.' The editor emphasizes 'compelling demonstrations of the efficacy of this new technique' and reviewers state 'the claims are justified by the data,' accepting the long-term stability claims without requesting additional validation.

result: Myomatrix arrays showed no voltage artifacts during movement, including at stride cycle contact points in rodent locomotion and during active arm movements in monkeys with peak speeds of ~15 cm/s and elbow velocities of ~40°/s.
evaluation: Reviewers accept the absence of movement artifacts as demonstrated. One reviewer notes that 'methods are explained clearly, and the claims are justified by the data.' The lack of artifacts during naturalistic behaviors is implicitly endorsed through reviewers' acceptance that the technology enables recordings 'during natural movement' and 'naturalistic behaviors' without raising concerns about artifact contamination.

result: Injectable Myomatrix arrays recorded 13 motor units simultaneously during reaching in rhesus macaques, whereas conventional fine-wire EMG in the same muscle yielded only a single trace reflecting an unknown number of motor units.
evaluation: Reviewers affirm the primate recordings as part of the compelling multi-species demonstration. The editor notes 'compelling demonstrations of the efficacy of this new technique in multiple animal species' and reviewers state they 'presented convincing examples of EMG recordings with high signal quality using this new technology from a wide array of animal species.' The direct comparison with fine-wire EMG in primates is accepted without challenge.

result: Myomatrix arrays successfully recorded from diverse muscle groups and species including mouse triceps (reaching, locomotion), masseter (jaw), rat triceps and digit flexors, optogenetically-evoked responses in mouse pelvic muscle, and muscles in cats, songbirds, moth larvae, and frogs.
evaluation: Reviewers strongly endorse the breadth of applications as a key contribution. One reviewer states 'they presented convincing examples of EMG recordings with high signal quality using this new technology from a wide array of animal species, muscles, and behavior.' Another notes 'the main significance of this manuscript is the application of this new technology to different muscles and animal species during naturalistic behaviors.' The diversity of demonstrations across species and muscle types is treated as a major strength.

result: Myomatrix arrays were fabricated using polyimide and gold layers on a carrier wafer, with 20-40 μm thickness, PEDOT:PSS coating on electrode contacts reducing impedance to ≤5 kΩ, and a fabrication pipeline allowing rapid development of multiple designs.
evaluation: Reviewers accept the fabrication methods without critique. One reviewer notes 'clear presentation of specifics of the fabrication and implantation, recording methods used, and data analysis' as a strength. Another states 'while technical details on the arrays have been published previously,' acknowledging prior validation of the fabrication approach. The methods are treated as adequately described and validated.

result: Motor unit waveforms were identified using adapted Kilosort 2.5 spike-sorting methods (band-passed 350-7000 Hz). The close electrode spacing in Myomatrix arrays results in sparser recordings better suited to Kilosort than traditional source-separation methods used for skin-surface EMG.
evaluation: Reviewers accept the analytical approach as appropriate. One reviewer specifically praises 'clear presentation of specifics of the fabrication and implantation, recording methods used, and data analysis.' The adaptation of neural spike-sorting methods to EMG data is implicitly endorsed through reviewers' acceptance of the isolated motor unit results without questioning the analysis methodology.

result: In over 100 Myomatrix injections in rhesus macaques, zero arrays broke leaving electrode material in muscle, representing substantial improvement over fine-wire approaches where wire tip breakage regularly occurs. Injectable Myomatrix devices appeared comparable or superior to fine-wire electrodes in ease of use and animal comfort.
evaluation: Reviewers accept the safety and usability claims without challenge. One reviewer notes 'the design included suture holes and pull-on tabs that facilitate implantation' as a strength. The zero-breakage rate in 100+ primate injections and favorable comparison to fine-wire methods are treated as credible evidence of improved safety and usability.

result: The songbird dataset included single-unit data from 8101 respiratory cycles collected over 74 minutes, with recordings ended by the experimenter rather than signal loss.
evaluation: Reviewers accept this as part of the demonstrated recording stability across species. The songbird data is included in reviewers' praise for 'convincing examples of EMG recordings with high signal quality using this new technology from a wide array of animal species, muscles, and behavior.' The extended recording duration is consistent with the accepted claims about recording stability.

result: Future applications of Myomatrix technology could include human clinical diagnostics, reduced risk/discomfort in clinical EMG, combining with muscle force measurements, and integration with brain recordings to reveal how neural circuits shape motor neuron activity.
evaluation: Reviewers accept these forward-looking claims as reasonable implications. The editor states 'this new muscle recording method has the potential to provide new insight into a wide range of questions in motor neuroscience,' endorsing the broad potential applications. Reviewers note the manuscript 'will be of significant interest to researchers in motor systems and muscle physiology,' implicitly accepting the proposed future directions as valuable.

result: The expansion of access to high-resolution EMG signals across muscle groups, species, and behaviors is the chief impact of the Myomatrix project.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly endorse this summary of impact. One reviewer states 'the main significance of this manuscript is the application of this new technology to different muscles and animal species during naturalistic behaviors.' The editor calls it an 'important paper' with 'major technical advances' that 'has the potential to provide new insight into a wide range of questions in motor neuroscience,' fully supporting the claimed broad impact.
